newsitem.title: EGYPT: U.S. pilot heads to Asia on Earhart tribute trip.
newsitem.headline: U.S. pilot heads to Asia on Earhart tribute trip.

text.p: U.S. pilot Linda Finch set off on Thursday from the Egyptian resort of Luxor to finish a flight round the world she says is a tribute to Amelia Earhart, the first woman to attempt such a trip 60 years ago.

After hours checking the aluminium fuselage of her 1953 Lockheed Electra 10E on the blistering tarmac, Finch ended the African leg of her 48,000 km (30,000 miles) journey and headed east into clear skies towards the Gulf emirate of Dubai.

"Amelia Earhart was an extraordinary woman in her time and the things she did were so unusual and so inspiring that it made a difference in thousands of lives," Finch, 46, told reporters at the end of her six-day stay in Luxor.

"I think clearly this flight should be a tribute to Amelia. What she did was so much harder, the things she had to conquer not having...navigation equipment and no one following to know. She spent her whole life working to inspire others and I want people to know that."

Earhart was the first woman to fly solo across the Atlantic in 1932. She had completed 35,000 km (22,000 miles) of her attempt to circle the globe in a Lockheed Electra 10E when she disappeared on the leg from New Guinea to Howland Island.
Finch, a Texan businesswoman with over 20 years flying experience and gurgling enthusiasm, said she became entranced by Earhart's life while looking for aeronautical challenges.

"I started looking for a new airplane and came across the Electra and in learning about Amelia, what she was like as a person, I got all involved in her and was so impressed by her that there was nothing else to do but do the flight," she said.

A few days after her 46th birthday in March, Finch set off from California in the United States to retrace a route similar to the one Earhart took in 1937. The journey has so far taken her to many places including Spain and Senegal and she is also due to touch down in Calcutta and Darwin.

Her stay in Luxor was one of four milestones on a trip expected to end in May. Memories of Earhart helped Finch brave thunderstorms on her 13-hour flight over the Atlantic but she said the Egypt leg has brought her even closer to her heroine.
"Going across Africa was very hard for Amelia because she had nothing to navigate by and there were so many vast areas that she didn't know where she was," Finch said.
"Again, coming across Egypt we had vast open areas where there are no landmarks to tell us where we are. It gave me a sense of what she had to cope with going across Africa."
Finch expects her flight from Honolulu to Oakland over the Pacific will take another rough 15 to 17 hours. But she says solid faith, sturdy equipment and talismans will protect her.

Proudly displaying a silver cross from her Presbyterian church and a locket stuffed with family pictures given to her by her daughter, Finch says she has no fear she will be unable to deliver what she says is Earhart's message.
"Amelia didn't like limits, the limits that society set on women in the 1930s... I believe the extraordinary thing that Amelia did was to show others that they could do it too."

Engine makers Pratt and Whitney have paid $4.5 million to restore Finch's 1935 Electra, set up an education programme and also for the two-and-half month "World Flight 1997" to 20 countries in five continents.
In spite of being fascinated by a different culture every few hours, Finch says she never loses sight of her goal.

"I really believe that Amelia as a person was just lost because of all the publicity of her loss. Nobody remembers what she was like. Everybody gets caught up with what happened to her that nobody remembers... She's a real heroine of our time, and we really want to focus people back onto her."
